title: Top-K Elements: Use a Heap Instead of Fully Sorting
oneLiner: Need only the K largest (or smallest) values out of n? A heap of size K finds them in O(n log k) -- without ever fully sorting the other n-k elements you don't care about.
keyTakeaway: Sorting the whole array to grab the top K wastes work sorting the n-k elements you're going to throw away -- a MIN-heap capped at size K (push every element, pop the smallest whenever the heap exceeds K) keeps exactly the K largest seen so far at any point, in O(n log k) instead of a full O(n log n) sort.
explanation:
The full-sort approach to "find the K largest elements" works but does more work than necessary: sorting costs O(n log n), sorting ALL n elements including the n-k you're going to discard. A heap-based approach only ever tracks K elements at a time. Push every value from nums into a MIN-heap (see Heap: Push and Pop): if the heap's size ever exceeds K, immediately pop its minimum. Since a min-heap's minimum is always at the top, whatever's SMALLEST among the current top-K candidates gets evicted first the moment a bigger element shows up -- exactly the behavior needed to keep only the K largest seen so far.

Using a MIN-heap (not a max-heap) to find the K LARGEST elements is the part that trips people up at first -- it's backwards from the intuitive choice. The min-heap's whole job is answering "what's the smallest of my current top-K candidates, so I know what to evict when something bigger arrives" -- that's a min-heap question, even though the overall goal is finding the largest values. (Finding the K SMALLEST elements flips it: use a MAX-heap capped at size K instead, for the symmetric reason.)

After processing every element, whatever remains in the heap -- all K of them -- are exactly the K largest values from the whole input, in whatever order the heap happens to hold them (not necessarily sorted, since a heap only guarantees the ROOT is the min/max, not full order) -- this lesson sorts them before returning so there's one unambiguous answer.

    # TODO: push every value into a min-heap. Whenever the heap's size

    # holds exactly the k largest values -- pop them all and sort ascending.
    return []

recognitionSignals: The problem asks for the top K, bottom K, K-th largest/smallest, or "K closest" out of a larger collection.
You're tempted to sort the whole array just to read off the first or last K elements.
gotchas: Finding the K LARGEST needs a MIN-heap (to know what's smallest among your current candidates, and therefore what to evict) -- reaching for a max-heap here is the classic backwards mistake.
Popping BEFORE checking whether the heap exceeds K (instead of after) can evict a value that should have stayed, shrinking the candidate set below K.
confusableWith: Heap: Push and Pop (Trees track) is the raw mechanism this pattern is built on, without the "cap at size K, evict the extreme" rule layered on top.

complexity.note: Each of n elements does at most one push and one pop on a heap capped at size k, each O(log k) -- better than sorting everything (n log n) when k is small.
